limitations: There is wide overlap in tumour size between patients who had curative surgery and those who did not - one patient with an 8 mm tumour was resected while a patient with a 30 mm tumour and no metastasis was not - so the two groups are probably not comparable
Follow-up duration differed between the groups and patients were not randomly assigned to conservative or aggressive treatment

Classification of surgery as curative or non-curative was made retrospectively from intraoperative findings rather than on an intention-to-treat basis, which probably overestimates survival after curative surgery

The actual metastasis rate may be underestimated because only 40% had an operation and 60% of metastases were identified by imaging alone; CT has low sensitivity for small pancreatic tumours and metastases in MEN1, and a cited study found 26% of patients with radiographically demonstrated lesions had preoperatively unidentified metastases at operation
Because follow-up after diagnosis was relatively short, the rate of growth could not be predicted and the rate at which tumours migrate from one size group to another could not be evaluated
critique: The 20 mm threshold the paper recommends is inferred from a metastasis gradient whose lowest two strata are 1 of 25 and 4 of 40 patients - rates whose confidence intervals overlap entirely - and the authors themselves report that survival in the 11-30 mm band was only slightly and non-significantly worse than at 10 mm or less, so the data support 'larger is worse' but not the specific cut point that subsequently entered international guidelines

The cohort spans 1956 to 2003 with prospective registration only from 1997, and the authors use the post-1997 subset for penetrance while using the whole cohort for metastasis and survival, so the two central estimates come from different populations imaged with different technology

Metastasis was imaging-defined in 60% of cases, and the authors cite evidence that a quarter of radiographically node-negative MEN1 patients have occult metastases at operation - which means the risk being weighed against the morbidity of surgery is systematically understated in the same analysis that recommends against surgery

Mean follow-up after diagnosis is 4.3 years in a disease whose victims die at a mean age of 43, so most of the hazard being adjudicated lies beyond the observation window; the 8-year survival estimates in the metastatic group have confidence intervals from 6% to 62%

The mortality argument is partly circular: life expectancy with a nonfunctioning tumour is compared against MEN1 patients without any pancreatic tumour, who differ systematically in age at diagnosis, screening intensity and era, and who by definition lack the lesion that defines the comparison

In MEN1 the pancreas carries a field defect with a mean of 2.9 tumours per patient, so a size threshold applied to the largest lesion ignores the remaining disease, and the authors' own data show 2 of 32 curatively resected patients needed reoperation for new tumours within 6 years

Thirty-two curatively operated patients and 66 unoperated patients with non-significant differences in metastasis, progression and death is an underpowered null, not evidence of equivalence; no power calculation or equivalence margin is offered
16432361.n: 108 MEN1 patients with isolated nonfunctioning pancreatic tumours, drawn from 579 registered MEN1 patients
16432361.bottom_line: In the largest population-based MEN1 series, nonfunctioning pancreatic tumours are the commonest pancreaticoduodenal lesion, reach 34% penetrance by age 50 and shorten life expectancy by about nine years, with metastasis rising from 4% below 10 mm to 43% above 30 mm - the basis for not operating below 20 mm, although that specific threshold rests on single-digit event counts, imaging-defined metastasis and 4 years of follow-up.
16432361.funding: Supported in part by a grant from the University Hospital of Geneva, Switzerland, to F. Triponez.

limitations: The study is not randomised; this is the authors' stated principal limitation

The 35 non-surgical patients did not have surgery for a mixture of reasons - refusal after discussion with the referring physician in 55%, concurrent illness, inability to consent, and the MEN1 size rule

The authors defend comparability by showing no significant difference in any clinical, laboratory or imaging parameter, including the factors previously shown to predict aggressive disease (sex, MEN1 status, disease duration, fasting gastrin, imaging results), and no difference in follow-up duration
critique: This is a gastrinoma study and almost all primaries were duodenal or nodal; it bears on functioning duodenopancreatic NET and not at all on incidental non-functioning pancreatic NET, yet it is the usual citation for the proposition that surgery prolongs survival in pancreatic NET

Thirty-five controls, of whom 10 were excluded from surgery by the MEN1 size rule and 5 by comorbidity, cannot be assumed exchangeable with 160 operated patients however many baseline variables match; refusing surgery after consulting one's own doctor is itself a marker of health behaviour, health literacy and access
Disease-related death in the surgical arm is 2 events, so the 23-fold difference and the 98% figure rest on single digits with no confidence interval reported for the ratio

Non-disease-related mortality was numerically higher in the controls (31% vs 20%), which is the expected signature of a sicker comparison group and undercuts the claim that the arms differed only in disease-specific risk; this is reported as non-significant rather than interpreted
Cause of death was adjudicated by the treating and operating investigators without blinding, in a study whose central endpoint is cause-specific

Controls were imaged every 6-12 months whereas operated patients were evaluated yearly, and controls less often had functional localisation studies, so ascertainment of liver metastases differed by arm in both direction and intensity

Accrual spans 1980 to the mid-2000s across three institutions while the operation itself changed mid-study - routine duodenotomy and intraoperative endoscopic transillumination from 1987, somatostatin receptor scintigraphy from 1994 - and all 10 patients in whom no tumour was found were operated before duodenotomy, so the arms are not method-contemporaneous
With 20-31% non-disease mortality over two decades, competing risk is substantial and no competing-risk analysis was performed; Kaplan-Meier censoring inflates the disease-specific separation
16926567.n: 195 ZES patients: 160 who underwent surgical exploration and 35 who did not
16926567.bottom_line: Over a mean 12 years of follow-up, routine exploration for gastrinoma was associated with far fewer liver metastases and a 15-year disease-related survival of 98% versus 74% without surgery, but the comparison is non-randomised with 35 self-selected controls, 2 disease-related deaths in the surgical arm, and no bearing on non-functioning pancreatic NET.

limitations: The pathology was not reviewed for this study, so Ki-67 or proliferative staining was not examined and could not be related to doubling time
Chromogranin A and other biomarkers were not examined and no marker data correlate with metastatic disease
Cut-offs of 1 cm and 2 cm were not analysed; only the 3 cm threshold carried over from the group's earlier work was tested
Some non-operated lesions diagnosed on radiographic criteria could on pathology turn out to be microcystic adenomas, although the authors state they do not look classic for that on imaging
The ultimate impact of this management approach on metastatic risk will only be known as the patients continue to be followed
critique: The three-criterion algorithm is derived from 9 metastatic events and then declared to capture all 9, so its perfect sensitivity is a tautology of the derivation rather than a finding, and no independent or temporal validation is attempted

Doubling time, the criterion with the largest apparent separation, could be calculated in all 9 metastatic patients but only 54 of 99 non-metastatic ones; patients with visibly growing lesions are imaged more often, so the exposure and the ability to measure it are entangled, and the missing 45 patients are simply absent from the stratification table

Sixty-nine of 108 lesions were never resected and their diagnosis rests on CT or MRI appearance alone - which the senior author concedes in the floor discussion could include microcystic adenomas - so a substantial part of the denominator is unverified, and any benign lesions in it dilute the metastasis rate downward
The study dates are internally inconsistent, December 1998 in the abstract against December 1988 in the methods, an eight-fold difference in accrual window that is never reconciled

The 3 cm threshold was carried over from the group's own prior publications rather than tested against 1 or 2 cm; a discussant asked precisely this and the author replied that the analysis had not been done, so the cut point in the resulting algorithm is untested within this dataset
No Ki-67, grade or differentiation data exist anywhere in the series, which in 2007 was already the strongest known prognostic axis in pancreatic NET

VHL PNETs are always nonfunctional, often multifocal and set against competing renal and CNS disease; with 2 PNET deaths among 633 screened patients, the algorithm is calibrated against a risk that is an order of magnitude smaller than the patient's renal risk, which the authors state but which also means the algorithm's clinical value is largely unmeasurable
The exon 3 association rests on 7 of 9 metastatic patients and is a single test in a cohort where exon 3 is already the commonest mutation site (50%), with no correction for the other exons examined
18063061.n: 108 VHL patients with PNETs among 633 VHL patients screened; 39 resected and 9 with metastatic disease
18063061.bottom_line: In the largest single-centre VHL series, 17% of patients had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour and only 8.3% of those metastasised; lesion size of 3 cm or more, an exon 3 germline mutation and a doubling time under 500 days together identified every metastatic case - but the rule was derived and tested on the same 9 events, doubling time was measurable in only half the non-metastatic patients, and two thirds of lesions were never histologically confirmed.

limitations: Functionality of islet cell tumours is not explicitly recorded in cancer registries, so functional status is probably under-reported; the authors note the functional versus nonfunctional survival difference would likely widen if all benign functional tumours were reported
US cancer registries collect data only on malignant pancreatic tumours; some hospitals in some periods were reporting tumours with benign behaviour and these were excluded for lack of uniformity
Tumour grade is substantially underreported for PNET (56.5% complete, versus 22.8% missing for pancreatic adenocarcinoma), and widespread applicability of the score requires better grade reporting
As with all large administrative datasets there may be miscoding, missing or inaccurate data, and pathological review of all specimens was impossible
The NCDB does not record MEN-1 status, the number of tumours within the pancreas, secretory hormone levels or the specific type of systemic therapy

Survival analyses based on retrospective data should be interpreted cautiously because of potential patient selection bias, particularly for surgery and adjuvant treatment, and the analysis of prognostic factors demonstrates association rather than causation
For patients who had enucleation and were reported node negative, nodal status was recoded as missing unless the number of nodes examined was explicitly reported
critique: The result most often lifted from this paper - that tumour size does not predict survival after resection - comes from a cohort in which only 19% of tumours were 2 cm or less and from which the registry had already removed every lesion a pathologist called benign, so the small-tumour end of the distribution is both thin and skewed toward the aggressive; the paper cannot be used to argue that size is irrelevant to the decision whether to resect a 1 cm incidental lesion

The score is derived and evaluated in the same 836 patients, with bootstrapping for optimism but no external or temporal validation, and a concordance index of 0.63 is barely above the 0.5 of chance; the authors defend it by comparison with a pancreatic adenocarcinoma staging system rather than against any threshold of clinical usefulness

Grade was missing in 43.5% of the cohort and nodal status was deliberately recoded as missing for enucleation patients, so the two variables that carry most of the score's discrimination are the two most incompletely recorded - and the 836-patient complete-case subset is by construction the best-documented 22% of the cohort

Pancreaticoduodenectomy emerging as an independent adverse predictor is far more plausibly perioperative mortality and tumour location than any effect of the operation, which the authors concede in the discussion while retaining it in the model and in the abstract's list of predictors

The cohort spans 1985-2004, during which WHO grading was introduced (2000) and 'neuroendocrine carcinoma' absorbed 'islet cell tumour' in registry reporting, so the exposure definitions shift within the study period

Disease-specific survival is unavailable, so relative survival adjusted for age, sex and race stands in for it; in a disease with a median age of 56 and 10-year survival of 38%, that substitution does substantial work and is not validated here

Only 1464 of 3851 patients had tumours over 4 cm recorded and size was missing for about 22%, so the null result for size is also a null result in the presence of considerable missingness, with no sensitivity analysis
18376195.n: 3851 patients who underwent pancreatectomy for PNET; 836 with complete data for all three score variables
18376195.bottom_line: The largest resected PNET series ever assembled established age, tumour grade and distant metastasis as the dominant determinants of postresection survival and found no independent effect of tumour size, nodal status or margins - but the registry excluded benign-coded tumours, grade was missing in over 40%, and the resulting score discriminates only marginally better than chance.
18376195.funding: K.Y. Bilimoria was supported by the American College of Surgeons Clinical Scholars in Residence program and the Department of Surgery, Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University. No industry funding reported.

limitations: Retrospective design with its inherent limitations

The exceedingly low median survival of untreated patients may be biased by late referral and more advanced disease stage, as the worse performance status, white cell count and CRP suggest, or by conditions such as age that precluded chemotherapy

Ki-67 was assessed by many different pathologists in different countries, so the 55% analysis may be biased by methodology, pathologist experience and Ki-67 heterogeneity, and the cut-off should be interpreted with some caution
Patients were not specifically reclassified according to the new WHO 2010 criteria
Response rates were evaluated by RECIST 1.0 from radiological reports rather than from measured scans
There are limited data explaining why the abnormal laboratory values evolve and what they reflect
critique: The 11-month versus 1-month contrast between chemotherapy and best supportive care is the paper's most quoted figure and is almost pure selection: the untreated group was twelve years older and half of it was PS 3-4, and a median survival of one month identifies patients referred at the point of death - the authors note this and still frame it as a reason to treat without delay

The Ki-67 threshold of 55% was derived by ROC in 42 randomly selected patients and then applied to the rest of the same cohort, so it is an internally generated cut-off with no external validation, and it disappears entirely from the multivariable model - meaning the paper's signature prognostic marker is not independently prognostic in its own analysis, a point the abstract does not convey
The regression that produces the final prognostic model runs on 170 of 252 chemotherapy patients after excluding the ROC derivation set and incomplete cases, which is not stated in the abstract

GI-NEC here pools oesophagus to rectum with 32% unknown primary; pancreatic NEC, the only portion relevant to a pancreatic pathway, is 71 patients analysed as a site subgroup with no multiplicity correction across seven sites

Small-cell versus non-small-cell morphology was taken from pathology report wording with no central review and no re-review of slides, which is the most likely explanation for the null result on morphology, yet the paper concludes the morphological classification is of uncertain clinical relevance
Response was assessed from radiological reports, not from measured target lesions, so the 31% response rate and the Ki-67 response gradient rest on unstandardised radiology narrative

Treatment choice between cisplatin and carboplatin was 'mainly due to different center policy', which makes the equivalence claim a comparison between centres rather than between drugs, confounded by everything else those centres did differently
The favourable 26-month survival in 36 patients with PS 0 and normal platelets and LDH is a post hoc subgroup defined by the model fitted to the same data
22967994.n: 305 patients with advanced GI-NEC (71 pancreatic primaries, 23%): 252 given palliative chemotherapy and 53 best supportive care only
22967994.bottom_line: The largest advanced GI-NEC cohort ever reported establishes performance status, primary site and raised platelets or LDH as the dominant prognostic factors and shows that tumours with Ki-67 below 55% respond less to platinum yet survive longer - but the untreated comparison group is a late-referral artefact, the 55% cut-off is internally derived and drops out of the multivariable model, and pancreatic NEC is a 71-patient subgroup.
22967994.funding: Nordic Cancer Union and Eckbo Foundations; H. Sorbye funded by the Norwegian Cancer Society, H. Gronbaek by the NOVO Nordisk Foundation, N. Holt by the Danish Research Council, E.T. Janson by the Swedish Cancer Society and I.H. Olsen by a Rigshospitalet research grant. The authors declared no conflicts of interest.

limitations: Retrospective data collection and a single-institution experience
Patients selected for observation of their tumours were not included, because the cohort was drawn from a surgical database

Reported complication rates were lower than the unit's own previously published rates and lower than the literature, and because they were collected retrospectively over two decades they are likely an incomplete picture of the morbidity of oncological resection

Ki-67 can be obtained on biopsy but biopsy is not always reliable because these tumours are heterogeneous, and the procedure carries its own risks; the two node-positive patients with tumours 1 cm or smaller both had Ki-67 under 20%
Given the indolent nature of many PNET, it will take several decades to determine whether limited local treatments compromise long-term outcomes
critique: The central claim - that no preoperative variable defines a group with nodal risk below about 12-20% - is generated from a resected cohort in a unit that states its own bias toward oncological resection, so the small, favourable, observed lesions that would populate the low-risk tail are structurally absent from the dataset; the authors acknowledge the omission but draw a management conclusion from it anyway
The headline 12% nodal rate in tumours 1 cm or smaller is 2 of 17 patients, a confidence interval running from roughly 2% to 36%, which cannot support or refute any size threshold

Nodes examined differed two-fold between head (median 15) and body-tail (median 8), and nodal positivity in this disease tracks with nodes examined, so the location effect is in part a detection effect even after statistical adjustment

Nodal status predicted disease-free but not overall survival (log-rank 0.1); the authors argue the OS result will become significant with longer follow-up rather than reporting the result they obtained, and then use the DFS finding to justify routine lymphadenectomy

Key predictors were fitted on incomplete data - lymphovascular invasion was known in 97 of 136, Ki-67 in 121, perineural invasion in 69, grade in 112 - so the odds ratios come from varying and unstated subsets
MEN-1 and functional tumours were retained on the basis of a non-significance test in a cohort containing only 13 and 8 such patients, which is far too small to exclude an effect
The complication rate (39%, 7% leak) is conceded to be implausibly low and incomplete, which matters because the whole argument weighs nodal yield against the morbidity of a larger operation

The recommendation that oncological resection be the standard operation for most patients cannot be derived from a dataset in which no patient was observed and no patient underwent enucleation without nodes except in 3 cases
24253141.n: 136 patients with locoregional PNET; 133 (98%) had nodal resection, of whom 50 (37.6%) were N1
24253141.bottom_line: Among 136 resected locoregional PNET, nodal metastasis was present in 38% overall and still 12-13% in tumours of 1-1.5 cm, and nothing available before surgery reliably identified a low-risk group - but the cohort contains only operated patients from a unit committed to oncological resection, the small-tumour estimates rest on single-digit event counts, and nodal status did not reach significance for overall survival.
24253141.funding: Statistical support from the Biostatistics Core, Siteman Comprehensive Cancer Center, NCI Cancer Center Support grant P30 CA091842; salary support for Y. Hashim from the Washington University Surgical Oncology Training grant 5T32CA00962124. Authors declare no conflicts of interest.

limitations: Cytology tends to underestimate the grade obtained on the resection specimen, so a low cytological Ki-67 should not be taken as proof of a low-grade tumour
EUS-FNA cellularity is variable and the needle may not sample the most mitotically active region, which the authors attribute to genuine intratumoural heterogeneity of proliferation
Only one resected tumour was cytological G3, which weakens the survival separation at the top of the scale
Neither a 2% nor a 5% cytological cut-off gave acceptable correlation with histological grade
Identifying that counted cells are genuinely neuroendocrine is difficult on dispersed cytological material
critique: The title advertises 'high reproducibility and inter-observer agreement', which is true only of two readers scoring the same slide; the clinically relevant question - does cytology predict resection grade - returned a kappa of 0.21 that the authors themselves call very low, and that result is not in the title

The concordance analysis can only include the 33 resected tumours, so the denominator is a resected population and nothing here tells you how cytology performs in the small lesions actually being watched
PFS was calculated 'independently from surgery', mixing resected and unresected patients in the same curves, so the cytological grade effect is confounded by whether the tumour was removed

The cG3 group that drives the significant PFS separation consists of 4 patients, all of whom the authors state were locally advanced, node-positive or metastatic at diagnosis, so cytological G3 may be a marker of stage rather than an independent grading achievement
The second cytology reader was a gastroenterologist, not a pathologist, while the histology arm used two pathologists, so the two inter-observer coefficients are not comparable
Fourteen years of accrual spans the 2000, 2004 and 2010 WHO classifications; the cases were retrospectively reclassified to WHO 2010 without re-review of the original diagnostic material
No adjustment for multiple comparisons across several cut-offs, subgroups and endpoints in 46 tumours
24750272.n: 46 pNETs in 45 patients; 33 tumours in 32 patients resected and available for histological comparison
24750272.bottom_line: EUS-FNA Ki-67 is highly reproducible between readers and a cytological G3 result reliably marks aggressive disease, but it under-grades G2 tumours in about 70% of cases, so a low cytological Ki-67 cannot be used to certify a small pancreatic NET as low grade.

limitations: The NCDB collects data only on tumours with ICD-O-3 codes corresponding to malignant disease, so these data may overestimate the malignant potential of small PNET
There is no explicit way to determine tumour functionality, so some functional tumours may inadvertently have been included
Multifocality is not reported in the database, so patients who had total pancreatectomy - suspected to have multifocal disease - had to be analysed as a separate surgical group

The reduced survival of the no-surgery group should be interpreted with caution because those patients may not have been offered surgery for unreported reasons that increased their mortality; the authors attempted to control for this by exclusions but call for prospective studies
Coding errors, missing data and the absence of key variables - mitotic rate, Ki-67, disease-specific survival and recurrence - all limit the analysis
Lymphadenectomy results may reflect inadequate nodal sampling, with a median of only 8 nodes examined and 27% of resected patients having none
critique: This is a National Cancer Data Base analysis, not SEER, and the registry by design captures only tumours assigned a malignant behaviour code - which removes the indolent small lesions a surveillance policy is about, so 29% nodal and 10% distant metastasis are a ceiling for a selected malignant subset rather than estimates for incidental sub-2 cm tumours

The arresting claim that 33% of tumours 5 mm or smaller have nodal metastases rests on a band of 94 patients in a variable that is missing in 45% of the cohort, with no confidence interval given; a handful of events in a selectively recorded field cannot adjudicate a size threshold

The survival analysis collapses 1854 patients to 366 by requiring diagnosis before 2006 and known surgery type, and then compares a no-surgery group that is older, far more often poorly differentiated and less often treated at academic centres against resected patients; the 27.6% versus 83.0% contrast is selection, which the authors concede in the discussion but still place in the abstract and conclusions

A 15% relative reduction in the risk of death for every later calendar year, during a window in which the authors themselves found no change in resection rates, hospital type or distant metastasis rates, is far more plausibly stage migration from incidental detection than improving care

The same calendar-year effect was not significant for 2004-2006 on Kaplan-Meier analysis, so the Cox finding is fragile and is explained away by appeal to greater model granularity rather than treated as the discrepant result it is

Nodes examined differ systematically by operation (63% vs 89%), so the finding that lymphadenectomy does not affect survival compares groups with structurally different staging completeness and is uninformative either way

The conclusion - that nonfunctional PNET of all sizes should be considered potentially malignant and resection considered - is drawn from a registry that cannot see the observed patients, cannot see Ki-67, and reports no disease-specific survival
24841347.n: 1854 patients with nonfunctional PNET 2 cm or less; 1367 with known extent of resection; 366 in the survival analysis
24841347.bottom_line: In a registry restricted to tumours coded as malignant, nonfunctional PNET of 2 cm or less carried a 29% nodal and 10% distant metastasis rate with no fall at the smallest sizes, and extent of resection and lymphadenectomy made no difference to survival - but the apparent survival benefit of any surgery over none is selection, and the metastasis rates cannot be transferred to incidentally found lesions.

limitations: The review is compromised by the moderate methodological quality of most primary studies
Most studies did not define delayed gastric emptying and only one applied the ISGPS definition, so differing endpoint definitions may have compromised the results

Selection bias cannot be ruled out given the absence of randomisation and the scarcity of baseline data in some studies; for most studies it is unclear whether the standard-resection patients would also have been suitable for enucleation
Long-term disease-specific outcomes such as disease-free survival could not be compared because most primary studies focused on short-term surgical outcomes

A planned subgroup analysis of enucleation in the body/tail versus distal pancreatectomy and enucleation in the head/uncinate versus pancreaticoduodenectomy could not be performed because the primary data did not separate fistula rates by location

All data come from non-randomised studies, so results must be interpreted with caution; a randomised trial of disease-specific outcome would be relevant but difficult because suitable lesions are rare, multicentre recruitment would be needed, learning-curve bias would intrude, and patient and surgeon preferences would impair recruitment
critique: The analysis most likely to change practice - that enucleation carries no excess fistula risk in high-volume centres - rests on 4 of 22 studies with I2 = 49%, and the volume threshold was defined by the authors themselves and inserted as a modified item into the Downs and Black checklist, so the least robust and least pre-specified result is the one carried into the conclusion

The primary comparison is between operations chosen for anatomically different lesions, and the review explicitly concedes it cannot tell whether the resected patients were ever enucleation candidates - which makes every difference in blood loss, operating time and pancreatic insufficiency partly an artefact of lesion size and location rather than of the operation

Means and standard deviations were back-calculated from medians and ranges by the Hozo method for an unstated number of studies, which manufactures precision in exactly the continuous outcomes where heterogeneity is already 50-87%

Indications are pooled across insulinoma, non-functioning NET, serous and mucinous cystadenoma, IPMN and chronic pancreatitis, so no result here is specific to pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, and the fistula risk of enucleating a soft NET differs from that of a cystic lesion
Exocrine insufficiency is reported as a pooled risk difference of -0.17 despite I2 = 86%, and rests on 5 studies in which the definition and timing of assessment are not standardised

The hospital stay result (-1.3 days) is acknowledged to be driven by between-country practice - 3 vs 5 days in the US study against 32 vs 34 days in the Korean study - yet it is pooled and reported as an effect of the operation

Only one of 22 primary studies reported information on principal confounders, which means the random-effects pooling is combining uncontrolled comparisons; the funnel-plot assessment of publication bias is uninformative with this few studies and this much clinical heterogeneity
The clinical question a surveillance pathway needs - whether enucleation without lymphadenectomy is oncologically adequate - is the one the review states it cannot address
26041666.n: 22 observational studies with 1148 patients: 432 enucleations and 716 standard resections (388 distal pancreatectomies, 328 pancreaticoduodenectomies)
26041666.bottom_line: Pooling 22 non-randomised studies, enucleation gave less blood loss, shorter operations and far less endocrine and exocrine insufficiency than formal pancreatectomy at the cost of roughly twice the pancreatic fistula rate - an excess that disappeared in four high-volume studies - but the operations were chosen for different lesions, the indications are mixed, and no oncological outcome could be compared.
26041666.funding: The Study Centre of the German Surgical Society was funded by grant 01GH0702 from the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research to 31 December 2013; the Systematic Reviews Working Group received a donation from Covidien. The authors declare no conflict of interest.

limitations: The 20% volume cut-off defining the high-grade component was chosen arbitrarily to ensure both components were sufficiently represented, with no biological basis for the cut-point, as the authors state explicitly
A minimal mitotic rate for the high-grade regions was not specified, although all cases had more than 10 per 10 HPF

When high-grade features appear in a small biopsy without the lower-grade component, morphological evidence of grade progression is difficult to assess and the diagnosis depends on prior clinical history
TP53 mutational analysis was not performed; p53 immunoreactivity was used as a surrogate

In the absence of a lower-grade counterpart the high-grade component can be morphologically indistinguishable from a large-cell PD-NEC, which matters for biopsy interpretation, and absence of gene mutations or altered protein expression would not resolve it
The explanation for high-grade regions - neoplastic progression versus epigenetic variation or multiclonality - remains open and requires ongoing genomic analysis
critique: The 31 cases were assembled by searching two pathology archives for grade discrepancy, which selects for the very phenomenon being described; the design cannot estimate how often high-grade transformation occurs, and the paper does not say how many WD-NET were screened to find them

The genotype claim that distinguishes these tumours from PD-NEC rests on four sequenced pancreatic cases, and the PD-NEC comparator genotypes are imported from a previously published series rather than run in parallel, so the key molecular contrast is between four prospectively sequenced tumours and a literature control

Survival is compared against historical institutional cohorts of 329 and 35 patients spanning different eras, treatments and staging practices, with no matching other than the single stage IV analysis

That stage-matched analysis is the result most corrosive to the paper's own premise - transformed tumours did no worse than grade 1-2 WD-NET once stage was accounted for - yet the abstract leads with the unmatched 55 versus 162 month comparison and calls the high-grade component associated with unfavourable outcome
Six of 31 cases are biopsies only, so the defining feature of the entity, a coexisting lower-grade component, was inferred from clinical history rather than observed in those patients
FDG positivity in 10 of 10 comes from 10 patients selected for scanning, and the mean SUV of 2.9 is low, so the imaging phenotype is derived from a convenience sample

Chemotherapy outcomes pool regimens, treatment lines, adjuvant and palliative intent and four primary sites across 21 patients, which cannot support the inference that platinum confers no long-term benefit
Ten of 31 cases are non-pancreatic, and the pancreatic subgroup that carries the survival and genotype analysis is 21 patients
26482044.n: 31 WD-NET with a high-grade component (21 pancreatic), compared with 329 low/intermediate-grade pancreatic WD-NET and 35 pancreatic PD-NEC
26482044.bottom_line: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours can contain a high-grade component that crosses the WHO G3 threshold while keeping the immunophenotype, DAXX/ATRX/MEN1 genotype and intermediate prognosis of a WD-NET rather than the Rb-deficient, p53-mutant, 16-month course of a true poorly differentiated carcinoma - an argument for splitting the G3 category, built on 31 archive-selected cases and four sequenced tumours.
26482044.funding: Partially supported by the Raymond and Beverley Sackler's Research Foundation and the Mushett Family Foundation. D.S. Klimstra reports speakers bureau honoraria from Novartis and is a consultant or advisory board member for Ipsen and Wren Labs.

limitations: Retrospective design

Relatively short follow-up of the observation group, which is why the authors stress that observation must be paired with a low threshold for intervention if aggressive features such as growth or nodal involvement appear
The question should ideally be answered by a prospective randomised study, which the authors judge unlikely to be accomplished given the rarity and indolence of the disease

Population-based data reaching the opposite conclusion are hard to interpret because registries lack familial status, growth characteristics, intent of surgery, margin status, comorbidity, performance status and consistent grading
critique: The inclusion band is under 3 cm, not 2 cm, yet this is a foundational citation for a 2 cm threshold; in fact the median lesion was 1.2-1.4 cm and 87% were T1, so the paper's evidence concerns tumours around 1 cm and is silent about the 2-3 cm range it nominally covers

Matching was on initial tumour size alone, deliberately leaving age, comorbidity, performance status and the surgeon's impression unbalanced; the observation arm was significantly older, so the two groups differ on the one variable most likely to determine who was offered an operation

The significant metastasis-free survival advantage for observation (99% vs 88%, p = 0.01) is an artefact of the endpoint rather than a finding: a resected patient can be recorded as recurring while an unresected patient with stable imaging cannot, so the two arms are not at risk of the same events; the authors report the direction of this implausible result without flagging it

A quarter of the observation arm had an operation and remain in that arm by intention to treat, so part of the arm's clean oncological record was purchased with the very surgery the paper argues can be avoided

The patients who were genuinely never operated were followed a median of 33 months, while the recurrences in the resected arm appeared at a median of 5.1 years - the observation arm was not watched long enough to experience the event the paper reports as absent
35% of the observation group never had tissue, so some lesions may not have been PanNET at all; those patients contribute to the 'no progression' numerator and denominator alike
Competing risk is material (6% died of other causes, median age 63) but is not modelled; Kaplan-Meier treats non-disease death as censoring and so overstates the chance of ever seeing a disease event
Fifty-one percent of observed tumours did grow, a fact visible only in a figure legend and submerged beneath an unchanged median size
Single tertiary referral centre with its own selection filter at the front door, and no accounting for the patients in the original 464 who were neither observed nor matched
26597365.n: 464 stage I-II PanNET reviewed; 104 in the observation group vs 77 size-matched resection controls (181 analysed)
26597365.bottom_line: In carefully selected patients with sporadic, asymptomatic, mostly sub-centimetre PanNET at one tertiary centre, initial observation produced no metastases over a median 44 months, but the cohort was under 3 cm rather than under 2 cm, a quarter crossed over to surgery, the unoperated patients were followed only 33 months, and the survival comparison favours observation only because the two arms cannot experience the same events.
26597365.funding: Funded in part by NIH/NCI Cancer Center Support Grant P30 CA008748 and R21-CA158267; all authors declared no conflict of interest.

limitations: Histopathological proof was not available for every detected lesion, so false positives are possible even though high SUV and location make most lesions likely true
The design is not a randomised controlled trial and there are no follow-up data, so it cannot show that treatment chosen on DOTATATE findings improved long-term outcome
Lesion count is only an approximation of tumour burden, not a measurement of tumour mass
The imaging denominator is not a perfect gold standard and may itself contain false positives
18F-FDG PET was not performed in every patient although DOTATATE is known to be less avid in poorly differentiated NET
Adding a diagnostic contrast-enhanced CT might have improved the sensitivity and specificity of both SPECT/CT and PET/CT
critique: The 'imaging denominator' is the union of lesions seen on any of the three tests, which structurally forces the most sensitive modality toward 100% and the others downward - a composite-reference incorporation bias that inflates the 95% vs 45% vs 31% headline

Only 25 of 131 patients (19%) had any histology, so the one analysis with an independent reference standard rests on a fifth of the cohort, and in it DOTATATE's per-lesion accuracy falls from 95% to 64%

The cohort is deliberately enriched for familial disease (MEN1 and VHL were an inclusion criterion; 14 of 25 operated patients were syndromic), so the detection figures do not transfer to a sporadic incidental pancreatic lesion
Pancreatic lesions are 12% of the lesion total; this is a GEP-NET and unknown-primary imaging study being cited in a pancreatic pathway

Reported pancreatic sensitivity of 95.5% sits uneasily with the well-documented physiological DOTATATE uptake in the pancreatic head and uncinate process, which the paper excludes for spleen and adrenals but not for pancreas

'Change in management' was adjudicated unblinded by the same multidisciplinary team that ordered the scans, is not a validated endpoint, and 32.8% is reported without any check that the changed decisions were correct
Single tertiary referral centre under an IND, with patients travelling to the NIH, so both the pretest probability and the quality of the comparator imaging differ from community practice
26712231.n: 131 patients; 891 lesions in the imaging denominator; 25 patients operated, giving 113 histologically confirmed lesions
26712231.bottom_line: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT finds far more GEP-NET lesions than 111In-pentetreotide SPECT/CT or cross-sectional imaging and often changes the plan, but the comparison is made against a reference standard built from the tests themselves, and the study offers no outcome data and almost no pancreas-specific or sporadic-disease evidence.
26712231.funding: Intramural Research Programs of the Center for Cancer Research, National Cancer Institute, and the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, NIH; all authors declared no relationships.

limitations: Small retrospective single-centre study whose findings, though intriguing, need prospective validation
The two PET scans were generally not performed on the same day, so shift in lesion position or size and rapid progression may impede accurate comparison, mitigated only by the 31-day limit
A novel grading system needs testing at other centres to establish practical utility and to measure inter-rater reliability
A larger cohort might have confirmed the prognostic significance of known determinants such as histological grade, whose non-significance here the authors attribute to the small heterogeneous sample
critique: Only 39% of the cohort had pancreatic primaries and the remainder span midgut, lung, thymus and breast, so nothing in this paper is pancreas-specific despite its use as a PNET imaging citation

Readers were given 'all pertinent clinical information at the time of scanning', which includes histology and disease extent - the very comparators NETPET is said to outperform - so incorporation bias favours the index test

The reported result is for a three-way collapse (P1 / P2-4 / P5); the 5-point scale that the paper exists to propose is never shown to be prognostic level by level, and several sub-grades contain a single patient (P3a n = 1, P3b n = 1)

A third of the cohort received PRRT, for which SSTR-positive/FDG-negative disease is precisely the eligibility criterion, and treatment is not adjusted for, so the P1 survival advantage may measure access to Lutate rather than tumour biology
The comparator, WHO grade, was taken at the time of original diagnosis - potentially years before the scan pair - while NETPET was measured contemporaneously, systematically disadvantaging grade

With 62 patients and a median OS not reached in two of three strata, the effect estimates carry very wide uncertainty; no hazard ratios or confidence intervals are reported anywhere for the primary analysis
No correction for multiple testing across several candidate covariates, two cohort definitions and two analysis strategies
28435454.n: 62 patients with metastatic NET (24 pancreatic primaries, 39%), selected from 730 DOTATATE PET scans and 118 patients with both scans
28435454.bottom_line: Dual DOTATATE/FDG PET summarised as a NETPET grade separated a group with FDG-positive, SSTR-negative disease and 11-month median survival from everyone else in a 62-patient mixed-primary cohort, but it is a hypothesis-generating single-centre analysis with no pancreas-specific signal and no adjustment for who received PRRT.
28435454.funding: Cancer Institute of New South Wales through the Translational Cancer Research Centre programme (Sydney Vital); D. Chan, A. Hayes and D. Bailey received support from Sydney Vital. Authors declared no competing interests.

limitations: The long inclusion period meant the follow-up programme was not standardised at the start - patients with raised chromogranin A were imaged more often and those with grade 1 node-negative tumours less strictly - which may bias the time at which recurrence was detected
The cohort is smaller than standard recommendations for Cox regression require; an unrealistically large cohort would be needed to meet those standards for this rare disease

Definitions of recurrence vary in the literature, some studies counting only distant metastases, and it is not yet known whether recurrence occurs more often locally or distantly, so whether the predominance of remnant recurrence here reflects selection bias is unclear
External validation was still ongoing at publication because of limited availability of adequate cohorts, and the authors chose to publish before it was complete
The role of resection margins remains unclear and surgeons must balance complication risk against the prognostic value of a more extensive resection
critique: The score is internally validated only, and the authors publish while conceding they could not find a validation cohort; the comparison that would justify its use - score versus WHO grade alone - returns p = 0.059, so by the paper's own test the score has not been shown to add to grading

The under-2 cm subgroup, which is what any size threshold needs, contains 4 recurrence events, and its univariable hazard ratios span two orders of magnitude (perineural invasion 3.19-295.74) yet are reported as predictors; no multivariable model was possible and none should be inferred

All three score components - grade on final pathology, nodal status and perineural invasion - are postoperative findings, so the instrument cannot inform the decision whether to operate, only how often to scan afterwards; it is nonetheless cited in guidelines addressing the operative decision

The cut-off of 24 was selected by ROC analysis in the same data by both Youden index and log-rank, so its 91% sensitivity is optimistic by construction and the 62% specificity is not clinically discriminating

Imaging intensity during follow-up was explicitly keyed to chromogranin A and to grade and nodal status, which means the score's predictors also predicted the probability of detecting a recurrence - a surveillance bias the authors note but do not adjust for

Excluding MEN-1, VHL, grade 3 and all metastatic disease produces a cleaner cohort than clinical practice presents, so the 17% recurrence rate and the 2-of-107 figure for triple-negative patients apply only to that filtered population

Median follow-up of 51 months against a median time to recurrence of 43 months means roughly half the cohort had not been observed past the peak hazard, and the 10-year survival figures rest on thin risk sets

Funding came from Ipsen, a manufacturer of somatostatin analogues, and the paper's stated purpose is to identify high-risk patients for future adjuvant therapy trials - a conflict that is disclosed but not discussed
28594340.n: 211 patients with curatively resected grade 1-2 NF-pNET, including a subgroup of 84 with tumours under 2 cm
28594340.bottom_line: Grade 2 histology, positive nodes and perineural invasion identify patients who recur after curative resection of grade 1-2 nonfunctional pancreatic NET, and 105 of 107 with none of the three stayed disease-free - but the score is postoperative, internally validated only, no better than grade alone at p = 0.059, and the sub-2 cm subgroup rests on four events.
28594340.funding: Funding for C.G. Genc was provided by Ipsen; the authors report no conflict of interest and no disclaimers.

limitations: The RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method carries potential bias in the selection and interaction of expert panel members, and panellist fatigue in addressing 193 detailed scenarios
The Ontario cohort has no data on WHO 2010 tumour grade (it spans 1994-2012), on ENETS or AJCC staging, or on margin status
As with all guidelines, clinical judgment and individual patient-centred factors and preferences must be taken into account when implementing the recommendations
Cost-effectiveness, resource use and patient preferences in the NET setting all deserve examination and were not addressed

The correlation between earlier detection and an overall survival benefit should ultimately determine follow-up recommendations, but this will be difficult to resolve in NETs given their low incidence, heterogeneity and extended natural history
No differences were recommended between R0 and R1 resections because no data on that distinction were available
critique: The two cohorts supplying the entire quantitative backbone were unpublished at the time of the consensus meeting, and the larger of them has no grade, stage or margin data - which are precisely the variables the resulting recommendations stratify on, so the panel stratified by factors its own evidence could not measure

The single most consequential statement, that grade 1 node-negative pancreatic tumours under 2 cm need no follow-up at all, is pure expert opinion at a 75% agreement threshold, in a dataset where cumulative recurrence reaches 48.5% at 10 years and median time to pancreatic recurrence is 7.2 years

Node-negative status in a small pancreatic tumour usually means few or no nodes were removed, so the exempted subgroup is partly defined by incomplete staging rather than by established absence of nodal disease - a circularity the paper does not address

The practice survey response rate was 15% (163 of 1068), and the clinicians who answered a survey about follow-up are plausibly those most invested in it, so the finding that existing guidelines are useless is itself subject to selection

Appropriateness was explicitly scored 'regardless of cost' while the discussion argues from resource allocation, radiation exposure and cost-effectiveness - the scoring instrument was blind to the consideration the conclusions invoke

The panel was drawn from the membership of the two societies issuing the guideline, and four of its own steering members wrote the 193 scenarios, so the questions and the answers come from the same group

Despite the 'patient-centered' framing, no patient-reported outcome, anxiety or preference data were collected or analysed; the single patient advocate's contribution is not separable from the panel vote

The recommendation against chromogranin A rests on one cited cohort of 100 resected ileal NETs, and the recommendation against chest imaging on an unquantified judgement that isolated pulmonary recurrence is rare
No consensus was reached on functional imaging, the fastest-moving part of the field, which leaves the schedule silent on the modality most likely to change it
30054622.n: 22-member expert panel scoring 193 clinical scenarios; evidence base of 6 studies (994 patients) plus unpublished cohorts of 936 and 129 patients; practice survey of 163 respondents
30054622.bottom_line: A RAND/UCLA consensus that de-intensifies the first three years after resection of a gastroenteropancreatic NET, extends surveillance beyond ten years, abandons biomarkers and chest imaging, and exempts grade 1 node-negative pancreatic tumours under 2 cm from any follow-up - the last being expert opinion rather than evidence, in a cohort whose 10-year recurrence rate was 48.5%.
30054622.funding: Funded by the Commonwealth Neuroendocrine Tumour Collaboration (CommNETS), which provided administrative support but had no role in design, conduct, analysis or manuscript preparation; conflict of interest disclosures: none reported.

limitations: GLP-1R imaging was deliberately compared with a standardised study MRI rather than with EUS or arterial calcium stimulation and venous sampling, so no comparison with those modalities is possible
Because inclusion required a pathological fasting test, specificity and negative predictive value of the tested modalities cannot be evaluated

Diagnostic accuracy and sensitivity are overestimated by the chosen reference standard: PET/CT showed a suspicious lesion in only 78.8% of all 52 patients, while the analysis set is the 38 who reached surgery and conclusive histology
In five patients (9.6%) imaging findings were inconclusive with lesions in different locations, which did not justify surgery and which a fasting test could not adjudicate
critique: Fourteen of 52 enrolled patients are absent from the accuracy analysis precisely because imaging was negative, discordant or surgery was declined - the denominator excludes the cases in which the index test failed, which is the classic verification bias of an imaging study with a surgical reference standard, and the authors concede it inflates sensitivity

The referral stream selected patients whose insulinoma had already defeated CT, MRI, EUS and in 13 cases ASVS, biopsy or surgery; the resulting 40% accuracy for prior external CT/MRI is therefore not a general estimate of those tests but an artefact of why the patient was sent to Basel
The index test was read by three blinded readers while prior external CT/MRI was read once at the referring centre, so the two arms of the comparison had different reading rigour

Surgical planning used all available imaging together, which makes the modality-specific 'impact on management' percentages unattributable; two of the patients counted as impacted (4 and 19) refused surgery and one (31) was a false positive

Six of 36 patients had MEN1, where multifocal lesions change the detection task and where PET's ability to discriminate insulin-producing from non-functioning lesions is a different claim from localisation accuracy

The sample size was chosen on 'a feasibility rationale and experience' with no formal power calculation, and the authors state that no adjustment was made for multiple testing across four modalities and three readers
Single centre, single radiochemistry facility, with the tracer developed by the same group - external reproducibility is untested
30054698.n: 52 patients enrolled; 38 with conclusive histology formed the main accuracy analysis
30054698.bottom_line: In patients whose insulinoma has already escaped conventional imaging, 68Ga-DOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT localised the lesion far more accurately and reproducibly than exendin SPECT/CT or 3T MRI, but the accuracy figures are measured only in the 38 of 52 patients who reached surgery and say nothing about specificity or about non-functioning pancreatic NET.
30054698.funding: Swiss National Science Foundation grant 320030-152938 and the Desiree and Niels Yde Foundation grant 389-12, neither with any role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Authors declared no conflict of interest.

limitations: The observational, non-randomised study design is stated as the main limitation of the study, offset in the authors' view by the long follow-up

The metastasis data require caution because only one patient per group developed liver metastases and the rate was obtained radiologically; the pathological rate is likely higher, since unsuspected locoregional metastases are found at surgery
No survival data were possible because no patient died; establishing the impact of early lanreotide on overall survival, treatment-related death and side effects will require much longer follow-up

Patients under active surveillance were more likely to undergo surgery, both for tumour growth and for the development of hormonal syndromes, and are therefore expected to have more often received systemic treatments other than somatostatin analogues and their complications
critique: Treatment was chosen, not allocated - lanreotide was 'proposed to all patients included, as alternative to active surveillance' - so the arms differ by whatever disposes a patient to accept monthly injections for six years, and the paper reports no comparison of comorbidity, MEN1 burden, prior surgery or stated reason for the choice

The primary endpoint is radiological progression under a definition that counts any new lesion reaching 10 mm or a 20% size increase; in a multifocal field disease this rewards an antiproliferative drug on the measure it is most likely to move while demonstrating no benefit in metastasis (one event per arm), functional conversion in the only two affected patients being an inference from 2 of 19, operations avoided (2 versus 5) or survival (no deaths)

The lanreotide arm carried more lesions per patient at baseline (p = 0.038), which the authors read as strengthening the result but which equally means more opportunities to register a per-lesion response and more lesions to shrink
Patient-level progression-free survival is mixed with lesion-level response counting (22 of 62 lesions versus 0 of 29) with no clustering adjustment for multiple lesions within a patient

Imaging was six-monthly in both arms but response assessment was unblinded, with no central read and no independent review described, in a study whose endpoint is a radiologist's judgement of a 20% change in a 7 mm lesion

Forty-two patients, 23 versus 19, with 17 progression events in total - and a p value below 0.001 from a log-rank test on that sample, with no multiplicity correction across the several secondary endpoints reported as significant

The two patients who developed functioning syndromes under surveillance, including a 20-year-old with insulinoma, would not have been prevented by lanreotide at the doses used and that inference is made anyway
The conclusion that somatostatin analogues 'delay or avoid pancreatic surgery' rests on 2 operations versus 5, a difference of three patients
MEN1 pancreata are field-defective, so suppressing visible lesions for six years may postpone rather than prevent the events that matter, and the study cannot distinguish the two
31586182.n: 42 MEN1 patients with pNETs under 2 cm (23 lanreotide, 19 active surveillance); 91 pNETs at baseline
31586182.bottom_line: The first prospective evaluation of a somatostatin analogue in MEN1-related pancreatic NET under 2 cm found progression-free survival not reached with lanreotide versus 40 months under surveillance, with a third of treated lesions shrinking, but treatment was self-selected, 42 patients generated 17 radiological events, and the metastasis, surgery and survival outcomes were indistinguishable.
31586182.funding: Partially supported by a grant from the Italian Ministry of Education, Research and University (PRIN 2017Z3N3YC_006); the authors declare no conflict of interest and nothing to disclose.

limitations: A potential pitfall of wait-and-see is late detection of disease spread, as happened in the patient found to have peritoneal metastases at operation; the sensitivity of CT, MRI and DOTATATE PET-CT for small peritoneal deposits is known to be low
To truly evaluate the oncological safety of watchful waiting, longer follow-up is necessary; only short-term findings are reported

As is common in investigator-driven multicentre studies, not all centres adhered to the follow-up protocol; EUS was considered burdensome and was frequently rejected by patients and physicians, prompting the study group to reduce the EUS requirement
The quality-of-life results are too premature to draw conclusions about the reason for the difference from the reference population
Patients with malignant tumour features were excluded from the study, which the authors note when interpreting the favourable course
critique: Seventy-six patients followed for a median of 17 months cannot support any statement about the safety of surveillance, yet the paper is routinely cited as the prospective evidence underwriting the 2 cm threshold; the resected series it is set against report recurrences at 4-7 years

This is an interim analysis of a single-arm cohort with no comparison group, no pre-specified non-inferiority margin and no stopping rule, so 'safe and feasible' rests entirely on absence of events in a sample too small and too briefly observed to generate them

The one genuinely informative event cuts against the conclusion: occult nodal and peritoneal disease in a tumour that was 2.0 cm on pathology is a 1 in 76 rate of under-staged malignancy at the top of the eligible size band, discovered only because the patient was operated

Six of the eight patients who met the protocol's own criterion for resection declined it, so the cohort's benign course reflects patient choice rather than the protocol being tested, and the protocol was in effect not evaluated

A quarter of patients were enrolled on a single imaging modality against a protocol requiring two, and 28-33% missed scheduled scans, so progression could have been missed rather than absent; one resected lesion was not a neuroendocrine tumour at all, which also means some surveilled lesions may not be

Eligibility excluded anyone whose lesion already looked malignant - exactly the population whose risk determines whether waiting is safe - so the study measures the natural history of lesions pre-selected as indolent

The quality-of-life signal, that patients enter surveillance with worse emotional functioning and insomnia than the general population, is the one patient-centred finding here and is dismissed as premature rather than pursued

Growth of 0.5 cm/year is used as the progression threshold without any evidence that it corresponds to biological risk, and two patients crossed 2.0 cm while their mean final size was 1.2 cm, so the threshold is detecting measurement variation as much as growth
33783475.n: 76 patients with a non-functional pancreatic NET of 2 cm or less
33783475.bottom_line: A nationwide prospective surveillance protocol for sub-2 cm non-functional pancreatic NET was implemented with no disease-related death at a median 17 months, but with 76 patients, poor protocol adherence, six of eight progressing patients refusing the mandated operation, and one occult nodal plus peritoneal metastasis at 2.0 cm, this interim analysis establishes feasibility and nothing about oncological safety.

limitations: The main limitation the authors give is availability: GLP-1R imaging is not yet authorised for routine clinical use
High and persistent kidney uptake of radiometal-labelled exendin restricts therapeutic use and raises pancreatic background
Quantification of beta-cell mass showed marked differences only in established type 1 diabetes, so GLP-1R imaging may not detect submaximal changes
Evidence for comparator tracers is called scarce and controversial, and no prospective head-to-head comparison with 18F-DOPA PET/CT has been done
critique: This is a narrative review by the group that developed, labelled and clinically validated the tracer, published in a supplement, and the comparative sensitivity table is substantially assembled from their own prospective studies

Table 3 places sensitivities from heterogeneous studies with different reference standards, different referral filters and different lesion sizes side by side as if they were comparable; several comparator figures rest on 5-13 patients, and the 18F-DOPA rows explicitly breach the review's own 12-patient rule
Diagnostic sensitivity in this literature is measured almost entirely in patients who reached surgery, so every number in the table shares the same verification bias and the table does not flag it
Receptor density figures come from in vitro autoradiography on 26-27 surgical samples, i.e. resected benign insulinomas, which cannot establish incidence in unresected or occult lesions
There is no evidence grading, no risk-of-bias appraisal and no quantitative synthesis, so a prospective crossover study and a case report carry the same typographic weight
The review contains nothing on non-functioning pancreatic NET, so despite being filed under pancreatic imaging it does not bear on the 2 cm observation-versus-resection question at all

The framing question 'will it make it to the clinic?' and the proposed algorithm are advocacy for an unlicensed tracer, and the stated aspiration that it 'will replace' ASVS is not supported by any comparative study of the two
34230073.bottom_line: A useful map of GLP-1 receptor biology and of exendin tracer performance for occult benign insulinoma and adult nesidioblastosis, but it is an unsystematic review by the tracer's developers whose comparative sensitivity table mixes incommensurable studies, and it says nothing about non-functioning pancreatic NET.
34230073.funding: Swiss National Science Foundation grant 320030-152938 and the Desiree and Niels Yde Foundation grant 389-12; the authors reported no potential conflict of interest, although they are the developers of the tracer under review.

limitations: Interpretation is limited by the lack of a comparator group and by the modest sample size
Because no other non-surgical treatment for VHL disease has been approved, designing a randomised controlled trial is an ethical challenge
The mechanism of possible resistance in the 2 patients with progressive disease is unknown, although a HIF-2-alpha gatekeeper mutation was reported in earlier preclinical and phase 1 work
critique: The 91% pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour response rate that gets quoted is 20 of 22 patients, a secondary endpoint in a single-arm trial whose primary endpoint was renal, with no pre-specified statistical plan for it, no multiplicity control across the several organ systems assessed, and no histological confirmation that each measured 'pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour' was one rather than a serous cystadenoma - the two were deliberately measured together in the larger 77% figure

RECIST response in indolent VHL lesions is several steps removed from the outcomes that matter - operations avoided, endocrine and exocrine function preserved, metastasis prevented, survival - and the trial reports none of them with a comparator

The comparison of 327 prior procedures against 3 on treatment contrasts a lifetime of accumulated disease across 61 patients with 22 months of follow-up; the authors' own figure shows 64 procedures in the preceding 2.5 years, which is the only like-for-like rate available and is not the one emphasised

Eligibility required no renal tumour above 3 cm, no metastases, ECOG 0-1 and gave a median age of 41, so the cohort is the fittest and least advanced end of the VHL population, and the authors note the contrast with the sicker advanced-RCC population in which hypoxia was previously seen

Anaemia in 90% of patients with 20% needing erythropoiesis-stimulating agents is a lifelong on-target toxicity in people who may take the drug for decades, and 22 months of exposure cannot establish durability, cumulative harm or resistance
The trial was sponsored and designed by Merck in collaboration with academic advisors, three authors are Merck employees, and medical writing was provided by an agency paid by the sponsor

Retinal haemangioblastoma assessment was explicitly qualitative, combining size, location, number, vessel engorgement, exudate and fibrosis, and the 100% improvement figure rests on 16 eyes in 12 patients

One patient was centrally assessed as stable while the treating physician called it progression, which is reported without resolution and indicates the softness of the response endpoint in multifocal low-growth disease
Nothing in this trial applies to sporadic non-functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, where the driving lesion is not VHL loss and HIF-2-alpha is not constitutively activated
34818478.n: 61 patients enrolled; all 61 had pancreatic lesions and 22 (36%) had pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours
34818478.bottom_line: Belzutifan shrank VHL-associated tumours across organ systems, with a 91% response rate in the 22 patients who had pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and no pancreatic surgery required over 22 months, but this is an uncontrolled secondary endpoint in a single-arm industry trial of 61 unusually fit patients, with universal anaemia and no data on durability or on sporadic disease.
34818478.funding: Merck Sharp and Dohme, a subsidiary of Merck; the Intramural Research Program of the NIH National Cancer Institute Center for Cancer Research; and NCI grant UO1 CA236489. Three authors are Merck employees; medical writing by ApotheCom was paid for by the sponsor.

limitations: The retrospective nature makes unintentional contributions of bias likely
Individual patients may be represented in both datasets because institutions in the USNETSG also submit reports to the NCDB

The NCDB does not report WHO grade, so exclusion of grade 3 relies on differentiation; the authors argue most grade 3 tumours are poorly differentiated so the analysis should still be weighted to lower grade
The indolent nature of PNET makes survival analysis difficult even with a median three-year follow-up
The low rate of recurrence in Black patients (3 events) limits meaningful comparison of disease-free survival between racial groups
Disease-free survival is not synonymous with overall survival, so no conclusions about patient mortality can be derived
critique: The policy-relevant cell is 7 of 30 Black patients with sub-2 cm tumours and the sub-1 cm claim is 2 of 8 - counts from which a recommendation to resect more aggressively by race cannot responsibly be drawn, and the validation cohort fails to reproduce the sub-1 cm finding at all (10% vs 9%, p = 0.66), which the paper notes but does not let alter the conclusion

Every patient in both cohorts was resected and had nodes removed, so this measures the prevalence of nodal metastasis among people already selected for an oncological operation, not among the surveillance candidates the guideline addresses - the very selection the paper criticises in the guideline is reproduced in its own design

Race is treated as a biological variable with no measure of insurance, income, referral delay, time from symptom to diagnosis or access to imaging, any of which would produce the same size-independent association between Black race and nodal disease at resection
The authors acknowledge the two datasets overlap institutionally, which means the NCDB 'validation' partly re-analyses the same patients and is not independent
Grade is excluded from one dataset and unavailable in the other, so the observed nodal difference may track grade, which is a stronger determinant of nodal spread than size

The recommendation runs opposite to this group's own prior USNETSG finding that node-negative Black patients had better five-year recurrence-free survival than White patients - a contradiction that is quoted in the discussion and then left unreconciled
Six size strata are compared across two datasets with additional regressions and subanalyses, with no correction for multiple comparisons; several of the significant p values would not survive one

The title's framing question ('are we undertreating Black patients?') presupposes that more resection is the remedy, when the same data are equally consistent with Black patients reaching resection later in the disease course
35380181.n: 453 patients (388 or 389 White, 65 Black) in the initial dataset and 5532 (4772 White, 760 Black) in the NCDB validation dataset
35380181.bottom_line: Among resected nonfunctional PNET, Black patients had roughly double the rate of nodal metastasis in tumours under 2 cm and tumour size did not predict nodal spread in them at all - a signal worth taking seriously, but it rests on 7 of 30 patients, does not replicate below 1 cm, comes entirely from an operated population, and offers no measure of access or delay to explain it.
35380181.funding: National Cancer Institute of the NIH awards T32CA229102 and K08CA234209. Disclosures: C. Yates receives consulting fees from Amgen, QED Therapeutics and Riptide Biosciences and owns stock in Riptide; F. Rocha is a paid consultant to Medtronic.

limitations: Inherent biases of a retrospective design could not be completely eliminated even with propensity score matching
SEER lacks important prognostic parameters including the Ki-67 index and surgery-related complications
The small number of patients remaining after propensity score matching may limit the generalisability of the results
Further prospective multicentric studies and more robust data are required to validate the conservative policy
critique: The signature finding - surgery improves overall survival while cancer-specific survival is identical - is the classic pattern of confounding by comorbidity and selection, not a treatment effect, and the authors nevertheless report the OS difference as a survival advantage of surgery in the abstract

SEER cannot distinguish a patient enrolled in planned surveillance from one never offered an operation because of frailty, dementia or advanced age, so the 'observation' arm is a residual category of the unoperated; the pre-matching table shows it was older and had seven times the rate of liver involvement

Functional status, symptoms and incidental detection are not recorded in SEER, so 'nonfunctional' and 'asymptomatic' are assumed rather than established, and some functional tumours are certainly included

The 2.50 cm ROC cutoff is derived and reported in the same dataset with no validation, and 'aggressiveness' is a composite of poor differentiation, nodal involvement, liver involvement and advanced stage - variables mathematically entangled with size and with each other, so that size is guaranteed to predict the composite; specificity of 63% would be unusable clinically
The exploratory 407-patient subgroup was selected using the Cox model fitted to the same data, so its null result is circular rather than independent corroboration

Propensity matching left 259 per arm and could only balance the variables SEER records; what it cannot balance - performance status, comorbidity, Ki-67, reason for not operating - is exactly what drives the OS gap

There is no imaging follow-up, no growth rate, no crossover and no information on surveillance intensity, so the paper has no purchase at all on surveillance as a management strategy despite its title
The paper misspells the central reference it reinterprets ('Ssdot et al.') and attributes Cherenfant's findings to Gratian, which is a sign of how closely the source literature was read
35923628.n: 5172 patients with PanNEN, 1760 (34.0%) with tumours 2 cm or less; 1621 NF-PanNET of whom 1350 had surgery and 271 observation; 259 matched pairs after propensity matching
35923628.bottom_line: A SEER analysis arguing that tumour size alone should not decide observation versus surgery for sub-2 cm non-functional pancreatic NET, but its central comparison is between operated patients and a residual unoperated group that was older and sicker, and the equal cancer-specific survival after matching points to selection rather than to any benefit of resection.

limitations: These are preliminary results; the study will conclude one year after enrolment of the last patient
Only a very low rate of tumour growth was seen after a median of 2 years, so longer follow-up is probably needed before definitive conclusions can be reached
The detection of synchronous liver metastases in four patients demonstrates a real, if rare, potential for distant spread among lesions of 2 cm or less
critique: The 20% rate of aggressive histology is the paper's most quoted and most consequential number, and it comes entirely from the 94 resected patients - a group selected for larger size, duct dilatation, younger age, anxiety and surgeon preference - so it cannot be read as the prevalence of aggressive biology among sub-2 cm lesions, and certainly not among the 406 who were watched

Conversely, the surveillance arm's reassuring course rests on 25 months of follow-up with only 2% crossover, so neither arm was observed long enough or exchanged enough patients for the two to be tested against the same risk; no outcome comparison between the arms was performed at all

Treatment was assigned by the referring centre rather than randomised, and enrolment at a surgical centre independently doubled the odds of resection, so a substantial part of what the study measures is local institutional culture

The conclusion that 'active surveillance is the preferred approach' is asserted in the same paragraph as the finding of measurable metastatic potential and aggressive histology in a fifth of resected tumours, without any analysis that could compare the two strategies
The metastasis rate is printed as 0.08 per cent when 4 of 500 is 0.8 per cent - a tenfold typographical understatement of the key safety signal, uncorrected

A third of patients never had an FNA and grade was not evaluable in a quarter of those who did, so there is no histological characterisation of the surveillance arm and the extent of under-staging there is unmeasurable
Anxiety (HADS 4-6) independently predicted surgery, which means some pancreatectomies in this cohort were treating distress rather than tumour - a finding the paper notes without pursuing
The study is funded by ENETS, whose own guideline recommending surveillance for lesions of 2 cm or less is the hypothesis under test, and the senior authors wrote that guideline
35986682.n: 500 patients (406 active surveillance, 94 surgical resection), from 540 assessed for eligibility
35986682.bottom_line: The largest prospective series of sub-2 cm non-functioning pancreatic NEN shows that 81% are watched and almost none progress over two years, but the 20% rate of aggressive histology comes only from the selected patients who were resected, the two management strategies were never compared, and 25 months is far too short to settle the question the trial was designed to answer.
35986682.funding: European Neuroendocrine Tumor Society; the authors declare no conflict of interest.

limitations: Retrospective design makes the study susceptible to bias, although consecutive series were identified at each centre
The scan interval of up to 90 days allows lesions to shift or grow, impeding accurate comparison, though the median interval was only 9 days against a median TTP of 17.1 months
The treatments individual patients received were not reported, which may bias both TTP and OS; in particular starting PRRT may confer a survival advantage on the P1-P4 cohort
